headline: A strong 10-year auction did not hold yields down for long: oil is back near $105 on record Hormuz tanker attacks and Hurricane Isaias, so the 10-year is at 5.33% again and stock futures are lower, while TSMC and Samsung just confirmed the AI chip boom is still accelerating.
summary: Stocks slipped Wednesday from Tuesday's records (S&P 500 down 0.22% to 7,801.77) as yields rose, then recovered off the lows after the $39 billion 10-year auction drew strong demand at 5.300%. The Fed minutes said most officials expect one more hike by year end, but gave no date, and Governor Waller said Thursday the hikes do not need to come at back to back meetings. Overnight, Brent jumped about 5% to roughly $105 on a record number of tanker attacks in Hormuz and on Hurricane Isaias, which is aimed at the central Gulf Coast with about 14% of US refining capacity near its path. On the AI side, TSMC's September sales rose 54.6% from a year ago and Samsung posted a record quarterly profit on memory chips. Today brings the $22 billion 30-year auction at 1pm ET; Delta reports Friday morning with fuel as the swing factor.

regime.why: Price is still strong (the S&P 500 sits 0.2% under its record and VIX is near 15), and AI demand data keeps beating. But the 10-year is back at 5.33%, the Fed says one more hike is likely, and oil now has two live supply shocks that feed straight into inflation. Hold leaders with stops; do not add size until the 30-year auction and the storm pass.

signals.title: The 10-year auction was strong, so the bond problem is oil and the Fed, not a lack of buyers
signals.what_happened: Treasury sold $39 billion of 10-year notes on Oct 7 at 5.300%, 1.7 basis points below the pre-auction level, with a 2.77 bid-to-cover and indirect bidders (mostly foreign buyers) taking 80.3%, well above their 72.4% average. It was still the highest 10-year auction yield since 2000. The Sep 15-16 minutes, released the same day, said most officials think another hike will likely be appropriate by year end. On Oct 8 Governor Waller said more hikes are needed but need not come at consecutive meetings, and the 10-year rose back to 5.328% with oil up about 5%.
signals.so_what: Yesterday's fear was that nobody would buy Treasuries above 5.3%. That fear was wrong: demand was strong. So the next leg in yields depends on oil and inflation data (CPI Oct 14), not on auction mechanics. Second order: as long as oil stays above $100, the Fed has cover to hike again on Oct 28 or December, which keeps cash yields high (good for cash backing puts and for brokers that earn on client cash, like SCHW) and keeps pressure on homebuilders, small caps and long bonds. Third order: a strong foreign bid at 5.3% suggests a ceiling may be forming if oil cools. What would make this wrong: a weak 30-year auction today (a tail above the 1pm ET pre-auction yield) or a hot CPI.

signals.title: Hormuz attacks plus Hurricane Isaias put diesel and jet fuel, not crude, at the center
signals.what_happened: Brent rose about 4.8% to $105.02 on Oct 8 after a record number of tanker attacks cut Strait of Hormuz crossings to a two month low (Kpler data cited by CNN). Hurricane Isaias, the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026, is forecast to make landfall Friday night or early Saturday between Mississippi and the western Florida Panhandle. About 2.7 million barrels a day, or 14% of US refining capacity, sits in or near the path; Chevron's Pascagoula refinery is closest. About 25% of Gulf offshore oil output was halted as of Wednesday, and US distillate stocks are the lowest for early October since records began in the early 1980s.
signals.so_what: Who pays: anyone who burns diesel or jet fuel. Delta reports Friday; its prior third quarter fuel assumption of about $3.15 a gallon already looked low before this jump, so the fourth quarter guide is the risk. What becomes scarce: refined product, because inventories were already thin. Who owns it: refiners outside the storm path (most large Texas and Louisiana plants sit west of the forecast landfall), which is why her MT Swing Setup scanner flagged MPC, VLO, PSX and DINO. CVX is two sided: higher prices help, but Pascagoula is the plant most at risk. Third order: product prices feed CPI and the Fed. What would make this wrong: the storm weakens or shifts east, or Hormuz traffic recovers; refiners have already more than doubled this year, so a lot is priced in.

signals.title: TSMC and Samsung confirm the AI chip boom is still speeding up, and memory makers hold the pricing power
signals.what_happened: TSMC said September revenue was about NT$511.86 billion, up 54.6% from a year earlier and down 0.6% from August; Bloomberg puts third quarter revenue near NT$1.49 trillion, above the NT$1.46 trillion analyst average. Samsung's preliminary third quarter operating profit was about 107.4 trillion won, a record and up 782.5% from a year earlier, with analysts estimating nearly all of it came from memory. One estimate has Samsung's phone unit losing about 1.8 trillion won because of higher memory costs.
signals.so_what: This is hard data, not guidance, and it backs up Marvell's and AMD's comments from earlier this week. The scarce thing is still leading edge wafers, packaging and high bandwidth memory, so TSM, MU and SK hynix keep pricing power. The second order effect is the cost side: memory is now expensive enough to squeeze makers of phones and PCs. HPQ shows as a buy zone on the dashboard, but its margins are exposed to this, so treat that verdict with care. What would make this wrong: TSMC's full report next week (Oct 15) guiding below trend, or hyperscalers trimming 2027 capex in late October earnings.

signals.title: Google pays Constellation to squeeze more power out of existing reactors, the fastest new supply there is
signals.what_happened: On Oct 6 Constellation signed a 20 year power deal with Google for 890 MW of new nuclear output from uprates at 11 existing reactors in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey (first one online in 2028), plus a separate 15 year supply deal for another 2,700 MW in PJM, backed by $4.3 billion of investment. The week before, Amazon signed a 690 MW deal tied to Calvert Cliffs. On Oct 5 We Energies agreed to sell Oracle 10% to 20% of the Point Beach nuclear plant's output, pending Wisconsin approval.
signals.so_what: Uprates add power years faster than new reactors and need no new site, so the hyperscalers are buying the existing nuclear fleet's spare capacity. Who gets paid: the fleet owner (CEG), and the suppliers of more fuel and bigger generators and turbines for the upgrades (CCJ for uranium, GEV for grid and generation equipment). Honest note: the dashboard says Avoid on CEG because the price is far above its fair value zone, and Congress members have been net sellers. The deal makes the story stronger; it does not make the stock cheap. What would make this wrong: regulators push the cost onto households (the deals were framed around the White House ratepayer pledge to avoid this) or uprate timelines slip.

signals.title: Boeing's $14.7 billion seeker deal shows where the missile defense bottleneck really is
signals.what_happened: Boeing announced on Oct 5 a seven year contract action from Lockheed Martin worth about $14.7 billion to triple output of the radar seekers that guide PAC-3 MSE interceptors. Some terms are not final and funding still depends on Congress. It sits inside the $53.86 billion PAC-3 modification Lockheed received from the Army in July. On Oct 7, ARK funds also bought drone and defense names KTOS and AVAV.
signals.so_what: An interceptor cannot ship without its seeker, so seeker output sets the pace for the whole Patriot program. Tripling it removes the main reason Lockheed could not deliver faster. Who gets paid: LMT as the prime, and BA's defense unit, about $2.1 billion a year if spread evenly over seven years. For Boeing that is helpful but not company changing, and the dashboard verdict on BA is still Avoid on valuation. Third order: more interceptors need more solid rocket motors and energetics (see the defense theme). What would make this wrong: a continuing resolution that stalls the money, or seeker yield problems.

signals.title: AbbVie's c-Met drug Temab-A gets two breakthrough tags, useful but early
signals.what_happened: On Oct 7 the FDA gave AbbVie's antibody drug conjugate telisotuzumab adizutecan (Temab-A) two Breakthrough Therapy Designations: with bevacizumab for refractory metastatic colorectal cancer, and alone for previously treated EGFR wild type, c-Met expressing non-squamous lung cancer. In the colorectal cohort of the first-in-human study, response rate was 15.6% and disease control 74.6% in heavily pretreated patients; at 2.0 mg/kg with bevacizumab (26 patients) median progression free survival was 5.6 months and median overall survival 9.8 months.
signals.so_what: For a clinician: these are small, single arm numbers in a late line setting, so the signal is disease control more than shrinkage. The real test is the ongoing Phase 3 AndroMETa-CRC trial against TAS-102 plus bevacizumab, today's standard. Breakthrough status buys more FDA contact and a faster review, not approval. For the stock it adds to AbbVie's oncology pipeline (now four antibody drug conjugate programs with breakthrough tags) while Skyrizi and Rinvoq carry earnings. ABBV is both a dashboard swing setup and in her MT Swing Setup scan. What would make this wrong: Phase 3 fails to beat TAS-102, or lung inflammation (interstitial lung disease), a known risk for drugs of this type, limits dosing.
